facts.text: Nishith Vadlamudi is a software engineer based in Bellevue, Washington (Seattle area), working on distributed systems, back-end platforms and cloud infrastructure.

Since January 2025 Nishith has been a Software Development Engineer at Amazon in Bellevue, WA, building distributed Java services and integration infrastructure on AWS for a large-scale fulfillment platform that processes millions of daily events.
He has nearly 3 years of experience building large-scale distributed systems and object-oriented Java back-end services, and he takes part in design reviews, code reviews, documentation and triage.

At Amazon he led graceful failure handling for a high-volume workflow platform: error aggregation and 8 close states in Java, TypeScript, AWS Lambda and AWS CDK, taken through design review and a phased rollout. It protects about 1,000 shipments a week from stuck workflows.

At Amazon he debugged a new API version that was failing 100 percent of calls, root-causing 9 routing, credential and serialization defects in Java services on SQS and DynamoDB, and it launched with zero client impact.

At Amazon he built an idempotent provisioning command-line tool with DynamoDB configuration, bulk runs and safe reruns, replacing about 30 minutes of error-prone manual setup per site with under 1 minute for all sites.

At Amazon he designed a per-API capacity model and a full-scale load test for AWS Lambda, ECS and DynamoDB services, validating 4.7 times the projected peak traffic with zero errors across 12.7 million invocations.

At Amazon he built a JWT-aware token cache in TypeScript on AWS Lambda (99.97 percent hit rate, cutting redundant auth calls up to 3 times) and DynamoDB batch-write retries with exponential backoff and jitter, closing a silent data-loss path.

At Amazon he automated deployment safety with AWS Fargate canaries, CloudWatch alarms and AWS CDK deployment gates, enabling automatic rollback in every production region; fault injection caught 5 release blockers.

At Amazon he took ownership of a routing service with little visibility and readied it for peak traffic: dashboards and alarms defined as code, limited retries with jitter, and a completed peak-readiness review.
From June 2021 to July 2022 he was a Software Engineer at ValueMomentum in Hyderabad, India, building enterprise web applications and microservices.

At ValueMomentum he built a full-stack workforce analytics platform with Angular, TypeScript, Spring Boot and REST APIs; SQL query optimization and better filters cut report generation time 50 percent.
At ValueMomentum he migrated over 10,000 client files into MS SQL Server with Java and JDBC through a phased, validated plan, without disruption.

At ValueMomentum he automated record closure with scheduled Java jobs and email notifications, reducing manual effort 80 percent, and rearchitected query processing in JWT-secured Spring Boot microservices on Docker and Kubernetes, improving query efficiency 40 percent.

He has a Master of Science in Computer Science from George Mason University (2022 to 2024), with coursework in analysis of algorithms, software architecture and design, secure software design, and machine learning.
Languages: Java, Python, TypeScript, JavaScript, SQL, Go, C++, HTML and CSS. Back end: Spring Boot, REST APIs, microservices, API design, event-driven architecture, JDBC and Hibernate.

Cloud and infrastructure: AWS Lambda, ECS, Fargate, VPC, DNS, API Gateway, DynamoDB, SQS, S3, AWS CDK and Terraform. Distributed-systems practice: caching, message queues, idempotency, retry and backoff, concurrency and fault tolerance.

Quality and operations: JUnit, Mockito, test-driven development, code and design review, load testing, OAuth 2.0, JWT, secure coding, Git, CI/CD, Docker, Kubernetes, canary deployments, CloudWatch, debugging and incident triage.

vidcite is Nishith's personal project: a question-answering system over Creative Commons tech talks on YouTube. Answers come only from the transcripts, every claim links to the second it is spoken, and questions the talks don't cover are refused.

vidcite uses hybrid retrieval (pgvector vector search plus Postgres full-text search, fused with reciprocal rank fusion) and a cross-encoder reranker, with Gemini writing the answer and Whisper transcribing talks. Timestamps come from the transcript, never from the model.

vidcite was built eval-first on a hand-labelled question set: the right passage ranked first went from 64 percent to 85 percent, 52 of 53 answers cite the right moment, 87 percent of citation links land on time, and 12 of 12 off-topic questions are refused.

While building vidcite he caught a silent failure: a reranker run matched the baseline exactly because every score was NaN, and sorting by NaN keeps the input order. After the fix the right passage ranked first rose from 64 to 79 percent.

vidcite supports voice: visitors can ask by speaking, hear the answer read aloud, and steer the video with commands like 'play the second one' or 'go back ten seconds'. A recorded demo is at nishithvadlamudi.github.io/vidcite and the code is on GitHub.

Othello multiplayer is a personal project: an Angular and TypeScript front end with Spring Boot services over REST and WebSockets, MySQL, Docker and JWT with one-time-password sign-in, syncing validated moves in under 100 ms, with 95 percent test coverage.

Concrete strength prediction is a machine-learning project: 5 scikit-learn regression models compared on 1,030 mix samples, with a random forest reaching 0.90 R squared and cutting error 51 percent versus linear regression.

Nishith is open to software engineering roles in distributed systems, back-end platforms and cloud infrastructure. The best way to reach him is email at nishith.vadlamudi.swe@gmail.com; he is also on LinkedIn (linkedin.com/in/nishith-vadlamudi) and GitHub (github.com/NishithVadlamudi), and his résumé is downloadable from this site.
Outside work Nishith is happiest on a mountain trail or inside a tricky problem, curious about how things work and why they break.

Resolve (AI Payment Dispute Agent) is Nishith's personal project: a Next.js and TypeScript workspace where Gemini investigates fictional payment disputes through typed tools, with Neon Postgres and a private PostgREST adapter. Code renders final explanations from validated records; the model cannot approve or execute refunds.

Resolve verification includes 194 key-free unit/API/UI tests, 35 live isolated Neon integration checks, and independently verified public Gemini investigations. Integer cents, scoped queries, database locks and unique execution keys protect the mock refund ledger. These are executed test counts, not coverage percentages or general model accuracy.

Resolve preserves its frozen synthetic evaluation: full-answer review passed 21 of 22 model cases and two deterministic guards passed separately. The remaining balance-limit explanation issue was fixed and verified on the public app; all 22 saved tool traces then passed deterministic replay, which is not a new model-accuracy score. The fictional-payment live demo and narrated walkthrough are linked from its project card.
